Senses.Explanation: You have gone and blinded the eyes of the whole city of Zhenzhou — Sansheng Huiran's verdict on Baoshou Zhao's opening-hall strike, raised and re-tried for seven centuries, every raiser asking who was really blinded. The earliest retained raiser states the strike and verses it. Wude of Fenyang: Baoshou opens the hall; Sansheng pushes out a monk; Baoshou strikes at once; Sansheng says — you help people like this? You have gone and blinded the eyes of the whole city of Zhenzhou — and Baoshou throws down the staff and returns to his quarters. Fenyang's verse: Sansheng shoulders Baoshou's spear; pushing the monk out to parley; the general beyond the passes enforces the true command — till blind men fill the whole Great Tang. Xuedou Chongxian, raising the same opening in his picking-old section: Baoshou and Sansheng, though they brought to light the Linji treasury of the true eye, only know how to lord it where there is no buddha. Had that monk been a man, the moment he was pushed out he would have overturned the Chan couch — and even then Baoshou's whole working would be three thousand leagues short. Yuanwu Keqin both raises the strike and re-speaks the line: Baoshou's whole-device shouldering is remarkable indeed, yet it holds only one side. Had he known how to bring forth the Linji treasury of the true eye, he would have waited for Sansheng to say — helping people like this, you have not only blinded this monk's eye, you have gone and blinded the eyes of the whole city of Zhenzhou — and then handed him plain everyday fodder. Why? One not-doing, two not-stopping. Liao'an Qingyu, at the Benjue temple hall: an arrow-splitting machine, a thousand-jun crossbow — true, the troops move as the seal turns, the general follows the tally; but what affair does it in the end bring off? He claps the Chan couch: south of the sky together with north of the earth — one lift, and all is gathered in at once. Huanyou Zhengchuan, in his probing-the-old section: this case is like meeting injustice on the road — it cannot escape the cluck of men's teeth. In the Tongyao the disputants number fifteen, all of them clear-eyed masters of their age; yet judged by right knowing and right view, one share in three is all they get. This must be known. And Mingjue Cong, opening the hall at Faxi: Baoshou's hand splitting Mount Tai, Sansheng's grip on the fiercest tiger — two old men carrying their poles, playing their show wherever they halt, well worth the watching; but say they prop the Linji true line — far, far too far. Why? You see only the waves surging; you have not yet seen the dragon palace beneath the sea.

Senses.Note: At Baoshou’s opening sermon, Sansheng pushes a monk forward, Baoshou strikes him, and Sansheng warns that such teaching will blind the eyes of everyone in Zhenzhou. Later masters dispute the warning. Wanru says he would expel Sansheng; Eryin thinks both elders still fall short. Linwo rejects familiar praise of their cleverness. Feiyin weighs the two as host and guest; Baichi would answer Sansheng with a blow of his own. Yun’e turns the old event toward his own opening. The city’s eyes name the stakes of a public demonstration, not literal harm.

Senses.Explanation: The image sets a slippery fish the unlikely task of climbing a narrow bamboo pole. Liao’an gives it for the relation between before and after seeing the fourth ancestor; Laona answers where an unnamed questioner’s words fell with it; Yuejiang uses it for someone arriving from Tiantai but going toward Nanyue; Huitang gives it as his manner of receiving people.
